questions.stem: Angela Green, 60, has a 10-day cough with rusty sputum and left pleuritic pain. You are examining her in general practice. Percussion is dull at the left base, so either consolidation or an effusion could explain it. Which finding at that spot best points to consolidation rather than fluid?
options: Reduced chest expansion on the left side
Tracheal deviation towards the left side
Bronchial breath sounds with increased vocal resonance
Stony dullness extending up into the left axilla
questions.why: Consolidated lung is solid but its airways stay open, so it carries sound from the large airways well, giving bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance. Fluid in the pleural space damps sound, so breath sounds and vocal resonance are reduced over an effusion.
notes: Reduced expansion on the affected side happens with both consolidation and effusion, so it cannot tell them apart.
Simple consolidation does not shift the trachea; it moves towards collapse and away from a large effusion, and this effusion is small.
Stony dullness that rises into the axilla is the sign of pleural fluid, not consolidation.

questions.stem: Angela, 60, 68 kg, has left lower lobe pneumonia confirmed on X-ray. She is alert, RR 22, BP 126/74, SpO2 95% on room air, urea 6.1 mmol/L, so CURB-65 is 0. She has no drug allergies and you and the GP agree to treat her at home. Which antibiotic regimen does eTG recommend?
options: Roxithromycin 300 mg orally once daily for 5 days
questions.why: For low-severity community-acquired pneumonia, eTG recommends high-dose oral amoxicillin, 1 g 8-hourly for 5 days, which treats Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most likely cause. Doxycycline is the alternative if she is allergic to penicillin.
notes: Adding clavulanate gives broader cover than low-severity CAP needs and causes more side effects; eTG does not use it first line here.
A macrolide on its own gives unreliable cover for pneumococcus because resistance is common, so eTG does not use it as first-line monotherapy.
An oral cephalosporin is not first line for low-severity CAP when there is no penicillin allergy; amoxicillin is preferred.

questions.stem: Angela, 60, a lifelong non-smoker, had a cold 10 days ago. For the past 4 days she has been coughing up sticky, rust-coloured sputum, and her X-ray shows lobar consolidation with air bronchograms. Her GP thinks pneumococcus is the likely cause. What best explains the rust colour of her sputum?
options: Haemosiderin-laden macrophages from chronic pulmonary venous congestion
Red cells and fibrin leaking into the alveolar exudate as the lobe consolidates
Bleeding from a tumour that has eroded a branch of a bronchial artery
Haemorrhagic infarction beyond an occluded branch of the pulmonary artery
questions.why: In pneumococcal lobar pneumonia, inflamed capillaries leak neutrophils, fibrin and red cells into the alveoli (red hepatisation). Breakdown of haemoglobin from those red cells gives the classic rusty sputum.
notes: Heart-failure cells come from long-standing venous congestion, but she has no features of heart failure and this is an acute febrile illness.
She has never smoked, has not lost weight and her X-ray shows no mass, so a tumour does not explain an acute infective consolidation.
She has no risk factors for PE, and her purulent sputum, neutrophilia and air bronchograms point to infection rather than infarction.

questions.stem: Angela's PA chest X-ray shows an opacity with air bronchograms behind the heart. The outline of the medial left hemidiaphragm is lost but the left heart border is clearly seen. There is also a small meniscus at the left costophrenic angle. Where does the consolidation lie?
options: Lingular segments of the left upper lobe
Anterior segment of the left upper lobe
Apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe
Basal segments of the left lower lobe
questions.why: The left lower lobe sits behind the heart and rests on the diaphragm. Consolidation there blurs the outline of the left hemidiaphragm but leaves the left heart border visible (silhouette sign). If the left heart border were lost, think of the lingula.
notes: The lingula touches the left heart border, so consolidation there would blur the heart border rather than the hemidiaphragm.
The anterior segment of the upper lobe is in the upper zone, well away from the diaphragm, so it would not blur the hemidiaphragm.
The apicoposterior segment is at the lung apex, so consolidation there would show in the upper zone and not near the diaphragm.
